items.prompt: Two buyers call NaiveInventoryService.reserve for the last unit at the same moment. What can happen?
items.answer: Both read one free unit, so both succeed and the item oversells
distractors: The second write hits a version conflict, so its reserve returns false
The second buyer waits on a row lock, then sees no units left
Redis rejects the second reservation as its counter goes negative
items.explanation: reserve reads a snapshot, checks onHand - reserved, then writes snapshot.reserved + quantity. Both reads happen before either write, so both checks pass and both writes claim the same unit.

items.prompt: ADR-0007 reserves stock with UPDATE inventory_item SET reserved = reserved + $qty WHERE id = $id AND on_hand - reserved >= $qty. What decides whether the reservation succeeded?
items.answer: Whether that conditional UPDATE changed a row
distractors: Whether Redis still lists the item in stock
Whether a SELECT run first had found stock
Whether the reservation record saved first
items.explanation: Affected rows determine success: the check and the increment are one atomic statement, so a row is only updated when enough stock is free. A prior SELECT would reintroduce the race, and Redis never authorizes a sale.

items.prompt: According to ADR-0007, what may Redis do with inventory in Bazaar?
items.answer: Cache the buyer-facing availability hint, but never authorize a sale
distractors: Hold the authoritative counter, with Postgres kept as the backup copy
Serialize all reservations through a queue, one buyer at a time
Store the reservation records, since those expire on a short TTL
items.explanation: Inventory truth is the database row with on-hand and reserved counts. Redis may cache the availability hint shown to buyers, which can briefly say "in stock", but the reservation is authoritative.

items.prompt: In ReservationService.hold, tryReserve succeeds but saving the reservation record throws. What does hold do?
items.answer: It releases the stock it claimed, then rethrows the error
distractors: It returns undefined and leaves the stock reserved until TTL
It retries saving the record until that write finally works
It returns the reservation anyway, with no stored record
items.explanation: The catch block calls this.inventory.release(itemId, quantity) and then throw error: a compensation for ports that cannot put the claim and the record in one transaction.

items.prompt: ReservationService.release is called twice for the same active reservation. How much stock is released?
items.answer: The quantity once, as the second transition from active fails
distractors: Twice the quantity, so the item then shows extra free units to buyers
None at all, until the reservation TTL has run out
None, because release only flips the record to released
items.explanation: release first runs reservations.transition(id, "active", "released") and only releases stock if that returned true. The second call finds the reservation no longer active, gets false, and returns false without touching stock.

items.prompt: Writes in Bazaar publish cache invalidations after they commit. Why does ADR-0006 still put a TTL on every cache entry?
items.answer: So an entry heals itself if an invalidation event goes missing
distractors: So the CDN can ignore invalidation events and rely on the TTL
So single-flight knows when to merge concurrent cache misses
So writes no longer have to publish any cache invalidations
items.explanation: Event-only invalidation risks permanent staleness when an event is lost; TTL-only allows predictable lies. Events give precise freshness and the TTL is the self-healing backstop.

items.prompt: A hundred requests miss the same key at the same instant through ProtectedReadThroughCache. How many times does the origin load run?
items.answer: Once, and every other request awaits that same promise
distractors: A hundred times, since every request records its own miss
Twice: one load, then a confirming re-read of the store
Zero times until the previous entry's TTL has run out
items.explanation: Each miss calls singleFlight.run(key, load). The first call stores the load promise in #inFlight; concurrent calls for the key get the existing promise. Each request still records a miss metric, but only one load runs.

items.prompt: An entry is past freshUntil but still before staleUntil. What does StaleWhileRevalidateCache.read return?
items.answer: The stale value right away, while one refresh runs in the background
distractors: The new value, once the caller has waited for the refresh to complete
undefined, so that the caller can load from Postgres by itself
An error, because the entry is no longer inside its fresh window
items.explanation: In the stale window read fires singleFlight.run(key, refresh) without awaiting it (errors swallowed) and returns entry.value. Only past staleUntil, or with no entry, does the caller wait for the load.

items.prompt: Why does ADR-0008 have the browser mint one key per checkout attempt instead of using the cart ID as the idempotency key?
items.answer: A cart may have several valid attempts, and the key names just one
distractors: Cart IDs are secret, and sending them on to the provider would leak data
The server cannot store keys, so the browser has to hold them
Payment providers reject any key that a server has generated
items.explanation: The retrier owns attempt identity: a declined cart can form a new, legitimate attempt, which must not be deduplicated against the old one. The cart ID stays a secondary guard.

items.prompt: IdempotentCheckoutService creates the order, then the process dies before payments.charge runs. The browser retries with the same key. What does the retry do?
items.answer: Returns the pending order as replayed, and still never charges
distractors: Charges the order now, because it is still in the pending state
Creates a second order, because the first one was never paid for
Fails with a conflict error, because that key has an order
items.explanation: getOrCreate returns created: false for the existing order, and the method returns { order, replayed: true } before reaching charge. Only the creator charges, so an order created by a crashed request stays pending and uncharged.

items.prompt: A valid payment.succeeded webhook is delivered a second time, one minute after the first, with the same body, timestamp and signature. What does PaymentWebhookHandler.handle do?
items.answer: Returns duplicate: true, because claim(event.id) now fails
distractors: Marks the order paid again, which is harmless to repeat anyway
Throws Invalid payment signature, as it was already used
Rejects it as stale, because an earlier copy came first
items.explanation: After the timestamp and HMAC checks pass, handle calls events.claim(event.id); the second claim returns false, so it returns { duplicate: true } without calling markOrderPaid.

items.prompt: What exactly does Bazaar's payment webhook HMAC cover, according to payments.ts?
items.answer: The timestamp and the raw body, joined by a dot
distractors: The raw body alone, as the ADR summary words it
The parsed JSON event, sorted by key
The event id and order id, joined by a colon
items.explanation: signPaymentWebhook computes createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${timestamp}.${body}`). Signing the timestamp is what makes the 5-minute staleness check meaningful. ADR-0008 says "HMAC over the raw body"; the code signs timestamp.body.

items.front: State Bazaar's cache key, tag and ownership conventions.
items.back: Key: bazaar:v1:store:{storeId}:{resource}:{id} (versioned namespace). Tag: {resource}:{id} for every entity whose change alters the projection. Owner: the committed write path invalidates after durable success. Layers CDN, ISR, Redis, Postgres. Catalog: 60 s fresh + 5 min SWR; admin/cart/checkout: zero staleness.

items.front: What does ADR-0008 do at the money boundary to charge once and charge the right amount?
items.back: One browser-minted key per attempt; the API atomically get-or-creates one order by that key and only the creator charges, passing the key to the provider. Before charge it revalidates catalog prices and active holds. Webhooks verify HMAC and atomically claim event ids; a decline marks the order failed and releases reservations once.

items.front: Which order status transitions does order-state.ts allow from pending and from paid?
items.back: pending -> paid, failed or cancelled. paid -> partially_fulfilled, fulfilled, cancelled or refunded. failed, cancelled and refunded are terminal; anything else throws "Illegal order transition".

items.prompt: ADR-0001 runs the storefront and the admin as two applications. What does it say one Next.js app would couple, and what does the split cost?
items.answer: Rendering mode, scaling and failure domain; two deployments plus package sharing
distractors: Auth sessions, cookies and CSRF tokens; two databases plus a sync job
Build cache, bundle size and test runs; two repos plus a release train
Route handlers, middleware and logging; two catalogs plus a merge step
items.explanation: ADR-0001 (lines 8-12): buyers send read-heavy, latency-sensitive traffic and tolerate bounded staleness, while merchants need immediate read-after-write consistency, so one Next.js application 'would couple their rendering mode, scaling, and failure domain'. The Consequences (lines 25-27) name the price of splitting: two deployments and deliberate sharing through packages instead of route imports. Both apps still share domain contracts and one catalog source of truth, so there is no second database or catalog.

items.prompt: Besides adding cache layers in measured stages, what does ADR-0002 require every cached surface to name?
items.answer: Its audience and how much staleness it tolerates
distractors: Its traffic tier and its personalization level
Its key version prefix and the tags it carries
Its owning team and the runbook that restores it
items.explanation: ADR-0002 (lines 22-24): 'Every cached surface must name its audience and staleness tolerance.' It then applies the rule: storefront catalog pages initially tolerate 60 seconds, while cart, checkout, inventory mutation and all admin reads tolerate zero. Traffic tier and personalization are columns of the separate rendering-strategy table, and key prefixes, tags, owners and runbooks are not part of this ADR's rule.

items.prompt: A merchant adds a new Color value to a product whose variants already exist. Per ADR-0003, what happens to the existing variants when the matrix is regenerated?
items.answer: Rows matching by sorted selection identity keep their IDs, SKUs and prices
distractors: All rows are dropped and recreated, so each variant gets a fresh ID and SKU
Rows are archived and copied forward, with new IDs pointing at the old ones
Rows keep their IDs, but SKUs and prices reset to the product's defaults
items.explanation: ADR-0003 (lines 15-19) stores one Variant row per option-value combination and matches existing rows through a deterministic, sorted selection identity, so matrix regeneration is a merge: matching variants preserve IDs, SKUs, prices and future inventory, new combinations get defaults, and removed combinations referenced downstream require an explicit merchant decision. Nothing is dropped, archived or reset to defaults for rows that still match.

items.prompt: Why does ADR-0003 reject storing a product's whole option matrix as JSON on the product?
items.answer: Each downstream domain would invent an unstable path into the document
distractors: Postgres cannot index a JSON column well enough for catalog filters
Large option matrices would exceed the row size limit of the product
Merchants could no longer rename an option once the JSON had been saved
items.explanation: ADR-0003's context (lines 8-11): inventory, price, SKU, cart lines and order lines all refer to one exact combination, and the product-JSON matrix 'forces every downstream domain to invent an unstable path into that document'. Explicit rows make variant IDs the stable atom of commerce with a real foreign key (lines 23-26). The costs the ADR does name are more rows and an admin managing a Cartesian product; indexing, row size and renaming are not its argument.

items.prompt: In the rendering strategy's decision sequence, a page that falls through to step 4 gets ISR. What must come with that ISR choice?
items.answer: A written time bound and an owner for invalidation
distractors: A recorded load test and a rollback plan for the route
A CDN purge hook and a static fallback for outages
A cache-hit target and a warming list for the route
items.explanation: The decision sequence (lines 14-17) renders dynamically when two buyers cannot receive identical HTML or the value cannot be stale, uses SSG when the page changes only at release time, and otherwise uses 'ISR with a written time bound and an invalidation owner'. Load tests, rollback plans, purge hooks, fallbacks, hit targets and warming lists are not what step 4 attaches to the choice.

items.prompt: What does Bazaar's rendering strategy say an ISR revalidation window actually is?
items.answer: A maximum expected age that a cached page may reach
distractors: An exact schedule on which every page is rebuilt
A freshness promise that checkout can rely on
A hard expiry after which the page returns errors to buyers
items.explanation: Lines 19-22: ISR gives static response speed and periodic recomputation, and its revalidation window 'is a maximum expected age, not permission to use cached data for money or stock'. Catalog pages may display bounded-stale price and availability, but checkout must re-read authoritative price, discounts and inventory, so the window is not a promise checkout can lean on, not an exact rebuild schedule, and not an expiry that produces errors.

items.prompt: Where does Bazaar's rendering strategy place the "use client" directive on a product page, and why?
items.answer: At the smallest interactive part, so the whole page stays out of the bundle
distractors: At the page root, so Add to cart can share state with every other section
In the data layer, so prices are fetched and formatted inside the browser
On every component, so the page can hydrate in one pass after it loads
items.explanation: The RSC boundary section (lines 26-29): fetch and format product and collection data in server components so it ships no client JavaScript, and place "use client" at the smallest interaction boundary, such as Add to cart, so stateful behavior does not pull the whole product page into the browser bundle. Putting it at the root or on every component would ship exactly what the rule avoids, and formatting stays on the server.

items.prompt: Under ADR-0005, what has to happen before Bazaar adopts a dedicated search engine?
items.answer: The 50k lab must show a limit, such as facet p95 above 150 ms
distractors: The live catalog must grow past 50k products in a single store
A vendor benchmark must beat Postgres FTS on median query time
Merchants must ask for synonyms and pinning on their storefront
items.explanation: ADR-0005 (lines 12-15) adopts a dedicated engine only when the 50k-product lab demonstrates one or more measured limits: facet p95 above 150ms, missing typo tolerance that harms discovery, relevance tuning too costly in SQL, or search load competing with OLTP capacity. Live catalog size, a vendor benchmark or a merchant feature request is not on that list; until then search stays a weighted tsvector with a GIN index, with Postgres as fallback.

items.prompt: ADR-0009 adopts a Typesense-shaped engine. What did the reproduced 50k projection show that triggered the decision?
items.answer: Latency stayed under the trigger, but a transposed query found nothing
distractors: Facet latency crossed the trigger, though every query still found results
Search load began to compete with OLTP writes during the peak test run
Relevance tuning in SQL took longer than the sprint had budgeted for
items.explanation: ADR-0009 (lines 8-11): the reproduced 50k pure projection 'stayed below the latency trigger (78.65ms p95) but returned zero results for a transposed query'; product requirements, not an unproven speed claim, trigger adoption of an engine for typo tolerance, native faceting, synonyms, pinning and relevance controls. Latency did not cross the trigger, and OLTP competition or SQL tuning cost is not what the projection showed.

items.prompt: A product event never reaches the Typesense index. Per ADR-0009, what eventually repairs the stale index document?
items.answer: Periodic reconciliation that compares each derived document and fixes drift
distractors: A TTL on each index document, so expired ones reload on the next search
A nightly job that drops the whole search collection and rebuilds it from Postgres
The merchant, who resaves the product to publish a fresh upsert event
items.explanation: ADR-0009 (lines 13-15): Postgres remains catalog truth, product events upsert the index quickly, and 'periodic reconciliation compares every derived document and repairs drift', with the drift count observable. Lines 19-20: search becomes eventually consistent, and reconciliation makes missed events self-healing. The ADR describes no document TTL, no drop-and-rebuild, and no reliance on a merchant re-saving the product.

items.prompt: How does ADR-0010 keep cart and checkout promotion totals consistent, and where do global and per-customer usage limits live?
items.answer: Both share one evaluator; limits live in one conditional mutation
distractors: Checkout trusts the cart's total; limits are checked by a nightly job
Each has its own evaluator; limits are read first and then written
Both share one evaluator; limits are kept as counters in the cache
items.explanation: ADR-0010 (lines 8-10): 'Cart and checkout use the same evaluator; checkout reloads current rules and claims usage atomically. Global/per-customer limits belong in one conditional mutation.' So checkout does not trust a cart total, there are not two evaluators, and limits are neither a read-then-write pair, a cache counter nor a nightly check.

items.prompt: ADR-0010's final combination policy is deny-by-default. What did Sprint 10 deliberately ship in its place, and why?
items.answer: Unguarded stacking as flaw #5, so Sprint 13 can demonstrate the abuse
distractors: Deny-by-default from day one, with Sprint 13 only adding audit logs
A two-code cap per order, until Sprint 13 measures real abuse rates
Stacking off for all codes, until Sprint 13 adds a combinable flag
items.explanation: ADR-0010 (lines 12-15): the final policy is deny-by-default (rules stack only when marked combinable, and totals never fall below zero or configured cost), but 'Sprint 10 keeps the unguarded behavior as flaw #5 so Sprint 13's adversarial probe can demonstrate the abuse before applying this enforcement'. Lines 19-21: until that harvest multiple eligible codes can produce absurd totals, and the flaw ledger plus a characterization test make the debt explicit. No cap or blanket ban was shipped.

items.prompt: Under ADR-0011, what caps the amount of a refund, and what carries the refund out?
items.answer: The unrefunded captured amount; an idempotent provider executes it
distractors: The original order total; the merchant approves and sends it by hand
The current catalog price; checkout reprices and refunds the delta
The amount still on hold; the inventory port releases it as credit
items.explanation: ADR-0011 (lines 10-11): 'Refunds are bounded by the unrefunded captured amount and delegated to an idempotent provider.' The cap is what was captured minus what has already been refunded, not the order total, a fresh catalog price or a reservation quantity, and execution is delegated to the provider rather than done by hand or by the inventory port.

items.prompt: A merchant's webhook endpoint keeps failing. What does ADR-0011 say happens to that outbound delivery?
items.answer: It retries with exponential backoff, then dead-letters after six attempts
distractors: It retries every minute for an hour, then is dropped without a record
It retries three times with no delay, then the merchant is suspended
It retries until it succeeds, since consumers dedupe by the order ID
items.explanation: ADR-0011 (lines 13-16): merchant webhooks are at-least-once; failures 'retry with exponential backoff and move to a dead-letter queue after six total attempts', and consumers deduplicate by the stable delivery ID, not an order ID. MerchantWebhookWorker matches: it dead-letters once attempt reaches 5 (the sixth try) and otherwise schedules a retry after 1000 * 2^attempt ms, so retries are neither fixed-interval, undelayed nor unbounded.

items.prompt: A buyer checks out in a currency other than Bazaar's settlement currency. Per ADR-0012, what is sent to the payment provider?
items.answer: The same rounded minor-unit quote and currency the buyer was shown
distractors: The base-currency amount, which the provider converts at charge time
A fresh quote rebuilt from the latest rate at the moment of charging
The formatted display string, parsed back into minor units on send
items.explanation: ADR-0012 (lines 8-12): build a buyer-currency quote from a dated rational exchange rate, round once, display it through Intl.NumberFormat, and 'send the exact same minor-unit integer and currency to the payment provider'; never silently display a conversion while charging the base currency. Line 22: buyers pay the number they saw and every quote records when its FX rate applied, so the charge is not re-quoted at a newer rate or re-parsed from display text.

items.prompt: During a flash spike, what activates Bazaar's signed waiting room according to the capacity plan's strategy?
items.answer: Checkout p95 over 500 ms or DB lock wait over 100 ms for five minutes
distractors: Checkout p95 over 2 s or database CPU above 90% for ten minutes
Any checkout error spike above 5% for one minute on the public API tier
Queue depth over 10k jobs or worker memory over 80% for an hour
items.explanation: The capacity plan's strategy (lines 7-9): for flash spikes, rate-limit automation and 'activate a signed waiting room when checkout p95 exceeds 500 ms or DB lock wait exceeds 100 ms for five minutes'. Stateless tiers autoscale on concurrency, p95 and queue age, and the database is pre-scaled for announced events; CPU, error-spike, queue-depth and memory thresholds are not the waiting-room trigger.

items.front: What read path does ADR-0001 give the storefront, and what read path does it give the admin?
items.back: Both apps share domain contracts and the catalog source of truth. Storefront: cacheable projections, with 60 seconds of catalog staleness acceptable in the foundation and transactional truth deferred to checkout. Admin: dynamic, authenticated, uncached reads with zero staleness tolerance.

items.front: Why does ADR-0004 reject fully dynamic and fully static catalog pages, and what image rules does it set?
items.back: Fully dynamic pages make every buyer pay origin latency; fully static pages make catalog size part of deploy time and stay stale until another build. Product images get stable dimensions, responsive sizes, and LCP priority when above the fold.

items.front: Map each route shape in Bazaar's rendering-strategy table to its staleness tolerance and rendering strategy.
items.back: Marketing/home (high traffic, no personalization): hours or build, SSG. Product/collection (high traffic, no personalization): 60 seconds, ISR. Cart/checkout/account (buyer-specific, high personalization): zero, dynamic. Admin (lower traffic, authenticated): zero, dynamic in a separate app.

items.front: Summarize Bazaar's search stack before and after ADR-0009.
items.back: Before: a weighted tsvector with a GIN index in Postgres, filters kept as a closed AST with deterministic fixtures. After: a Typesense-shaped engine whose clients belong only in runtime wiring, which makes search eventually consistent and operationally heavier. Elasticsearch remains a future trigger for substantially more complex scale or analysis.

items.front: What shape does ADR-0010 give promotion evaluation, and what does that shape buy?
items.back: Pure integer-money functions over a closed eligibility AST. The math is exhaustively testable, merchant controls remain structured, and the order of application is visible.

items.front: What does ADR-0011's design let Bazaar recover from, and where do its inventory and refund invariants live?
items.back: Crashes between external calls and acknowledgements, without pretending that exactly-once network delivery exists. Inventory and refund invariants live at atomic persistence boundaries rather than in UI flows.

items.front: What does ADR-0012 give every indexable locale URL, and how is checkout accessibility checked?
items.back: One canonical, hreflang alternates, sitemap discovery, and Product/Offer/BreadcrumbList JSON-LD; transactional routes stay out of robots, and UI locales are routed explicitly with externalized strings. Accessibility automation gates checkout, but keyboard, focus, live status, semantics and visual contrast still need browser or manual review.

items.front: Give the capacity plan's budget and action for storefront p95, checkout success, cache hit ratio, inventory drift and oldest order job.
items.back: Storefront p95 under 250 ms cached: scale stateless, inspect cache. Checkout success at least 99.5% over 30 days: page below 98% over 5 minutes at 100 attempts. Cache hit ratio at least 90%: warm head and trends, inspect invalidation. Inventory drift 0 units: pause the SKU and reconcile immediately. Oldest order job under 60 s: isolate poison jobs, scale healthy workers.
